title: Oval-shaped resonance distortion as a signature of quasiparticle heating effect in a niobium superconducting resonator
authors: Zhenyuan Sun, Genting Dai, Xiao Geng, Liangliang Yang, Mingjun Cheng, Qing Yu, Jinlin Chang, Yi Yang, Linpan Jiang, Jianshe Liu, Wei Chen
abstract: We investigate the nonlinear behavior of a superconducting microwave resonator subjected to a dissipative mechanism where the associated quality factor (Q factor) decreases with increasing dissipated power, leading to a dissipative feedback effect. By modifying the Rothwarf-Taylor equations, we establish a macroscopic quasiparticle heating (QPH) model that directly links the quality factor to the microwave readout power. The key finding is the identification of a distinctive oval-shaped distortion in the resonance circle in the complex plane. This distortion serves as a practical experimental signature for identifying the readout power regime in which QPH dominates the loss, under conditions where other nonlinear mechanisms are sufficiently weak. To validate the model, we design and fabricate a niobium (Nb) half-wavelength coplanar waveguide (CPW) resonator and conduct systematic bath temperature and readout power sweeps. The model provides a well fit to the observed oval-shaped resonance circle distortion across a wide range of operating conditions, confirming the QPH mechanism as the primary source of the dissipative non-linearity in the parameter space investigated.
summary: This paper develops and validates a theoretical model describing quasiparticle heating losses in superconducting microwave resonators. By analyzing the resulting nonlinear changes in resonance response, the authors identify a unique 'oval-shaped distortion' in the complex plane as a definitive experimental signature for diagnosing when QPH dominates energy dissipation.
main_problem: The study investigates the nonlinear behavior of superconducting microwave resonators caused by quasiparticle heating (QPH) effects.
main_result: A distinctive oval-shaped distortion in the resonance circle plotted in the complex plane serves as a practical and reliable experimental signature for identifying the QPH-dominated loss regime.
method: The authors combine theoretical modeling, modifying Rothwarf-Taylor equations to create a macroscopic QPH model, with systematic experimental measurements using VNA sweeps of readout power and bath temperature.
model_or_system: The system is a Niobium (Nb) superconducting half-wavelength coplanar waveguide (CPW) resonator. The theory models the quasiparticle density evolution by modifying Rothwarf-Taylor equations to link the quality factor ($Q$) directly to the microwave readout power ($P_r$).
key_observables: The primary observables are the $S_{21}$ transmission parameter trajectory in the Argand complex plane, and the extracted internal quality factor ($Q_i/Q_c$) as a function of readout power.
important_parameters: Key regimes include the low-power thermal saturation limit and the high-power universal scaling regime ($u \propto P_r^{1/3}$), alongside bath temperature ($T_b$) and readout power ($P_r$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes that QPH is the dominant source of dissipative non-linearity in the investigated parameter space, allowing for a simplified analysis based on modified Rothwarf-Taylor equations.
figures_summary: Figures show numerical solutions of the governing quartic equation and experimental $S_{21}$ loci in the Argand plane. These figures illustrate the characteristic oval distortion developing as QPH losses become dominant over other loss mechanisms.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a theoretical model by modifying Rothwarf-Taylor equations to link $Q$ to power via quasiparticle heating. It then analyzes this theory using numerical solutions and validates it through systematic experimental measurements of the resonance response across varying temperatures and powers, culminating in the identification of the diagnostic signature.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, measurable spectroscopic tool (the oval distortion) to diagnose fundamental non-equilibrium energy loss mechanisms (QPH) in superconducting circuits, which is crucial for designing high-performance quantum devices.

Fig.1(a) shows the normalised quasiparticle density u, and Fig.1(b) the normalised internal quality factor Qi/Qc. Here, Qother/Qc = 108 corresponds to the regime where other losses have no influence on the dissipative behaviour of the device. Several features are noteworthy. At low readout power γ, the quasiparticle density saturates at the thermal floor u →uth, and Qi/Qc correspondingly exhibits a constant plateau whose level is set by the bath temperature.
